title: The other World Cup
author: Darren Coughlan
text:
Pacific Islands, explained.Therese Aiton of Papua New Guinea breaks with the ball during the 2022 Women’s Rugby League World Cup Semi-Final match between Australia and Papua New Guinea in York, England (George Wood/Getty Images)
The other World CupIn the contest over women’s sport in the Pacific, the scoreboard matters much less than the outcome.Darren Coughlan17 August 20264 min read|The other World CupThe other World CupIn nine weeks, the Rugby League World Cup (Opens in new window) opens across Australia, Papua New Guinea and New Zealand, with the men’s, women’s and wheelchair tournaments running side by side. Most of the attention will follow the men. Most of the money already has: the PNG Chiefs, underwritten by $600 million in Australian funding over ten years (Opens in new window), have spent 2026 signing marquee names (Opens in new window) for their 2028 debut in the NRL competition.But the sharper test of Australia’s Pacific sport statecraft will play out with far less noise. It is the women’s tournament.Canberra’s investment will not ultimately be judged by whether a franchise wins premierships. It will be judged by whether Pacific women can now play, earn and lead in the game Papua New Guinea calls its own. The Lowy Institute’s Serena Sasingian argued in The Interpreter in March (Opens in new window) that the design of the Chiefs project will determine its legacy. She is right, and the women’s game is where design is tested first, because it is where the least existed and the most had to be built. October is the audit.The encouraging news is that something real is being built. The Santos Cup (Opens in new window), Papua New Guinea’s first national women’s rugby league competition, is mid-season right now: six provincial franchises, an extended preseason, tiered player contracts, and fixtures stretching from Port Moresby to Rabaul, backed by PacificAus Sports. Five of its head and assistant coaches (Opens in new window) this season are women, among them Orchid No. 1 Cathy Neap, a sign that playing careers now convert into leadership.China’s stadium diplomacy handed Honiara a 10,000-seat ... Australia is betting instead on the people who fill grounds like it.Across the region, the title-winning Fijiana Drua compete in Australia’s Super W, while the Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade’s Team Up (Opens in new window) portfolio of over 35 sport-for-development partnerships engaged more than 112,000 Pacific Islanders in its most recent reported year, with women and girls holding steady at 42% to 47% of participants (Opens in new window). This is patient, human infrastructure. China’s stadium diplomacy handed Honiara a 10,000-seat arena (Opens in new window) for the 2023 Pacific Games. Australia is betting instead on the people who fill grounds like it.The 10,000-seat sports stadium built by China in Honiara, Solomon Islands (Charley Piringi/AFP via Getty Images) The research record says this work is worth doing, provided it is done without illusions. An umbrella review of violence prevention interventions (Opens in new window) found sport-based programs produced the strongest effects of any approach. Yet reviews of sport-for-development (Opens in new window) consistently locate the gains at the individual level, in confidence, skills and income, and can point to no documented case of a sport program shifting gender equality at the structural level. Even the field’s most rigorous trial (Opens in new window), a football-based program in Peru, cut partner violence against adolescent girls by 75% even as inequitable gender attitudes rose, a reminder that progress is rarely linear. The most recent Pacific evidence, from Fiji (Opens in new window), shows sport operating as a gendered livelihood pathway, with women’s participation squeezed by domestic responsibilities and community norms. And sport is not automatically a safe place for women: studies report that 26% to 74% of women in sport (Opens in new window) experience gender-based interpersonal violence. Pathways without safeguarding can harm the people they are built to serve.That is where the imbalance bites. Within the $600 million package, $250 million is earmarked (Opens in new window) for development and community programs across Papua New Guinea, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga. Yet Team Up, the flagship program doing the daily work of participation and inclusion across the region, runs on roughly $6 million a year (Opens in new window). A 2025 audit (Opens in new window) by the Gendered Violence Research Network at the University of New South Wales mapped 31 violence prevention programs delivered through Australian sport and found persistent gaps for First Nations, culturally diverse and remote communities, alongside a reliance on volunteers asked to carry safeguarding without training. The soft power literature (Opens in new window) adds its own warning: the feel-good effects of a tournament are real but perishable, and they convert into influence only when they are institutionalised.So institutionalise them. Before the first whistle in October, Canberra should announce a single measure: ring-fence 5% of every major elite sport diplomacy investment for women’s community competition and independent safeguarding, co-designed and delivered through Pacific bodies, not administered from Australia. On the PNG package alone that is $30 million, five times Team Up’s annual budget and a rounding error against the franchise spend. The machinery already exists: the Sports Diplomacy Strategy 2032+ (Opens in new window) commits Australia to partnership of exactly this kind, and the Sports Diplomacy Consultative Group is the obvious table at which to design it. What is missing is ring-fenced money and Pacific hands on the wheel. The World Cup gives the announcement a stage and a deadline.The Santos Cup grand final will be decided at Port Moresby’s National Football Stadium on 13 September. Five weeks later, the women’s World Cup arrives at the same ground. That is what a pathway looks like when it works: a girl can watch the Dabaris in September and the Orchids in October and see a future in both.Papua New Guineans will be watching a team, not a strategy, and that is exactly as it should be. But the result that matters most to Canberra will not be on the scoreboard. It will be whether, five years from now, a young woman in Lae or Suva still has a competition to join, a contract worth signing and a game that is safe to play.Sport off fieldAt the World Cup, as in life, football nationalises success and ethnicises failureOpinion by Abhinandan KumarAbout the authorDarren CoughlanDarren Coughlan is Discipline Lead Lecturer in Sport Management at the International College of Management, Sydney, and consults to sport and public-purpose organisations on high performance, governance, integrity and athlete wellbeing.TopicsPacific IslandsGender & equalityPapua New GuineaAustraliaSoft powerThe Interpreter on Pacific IslandsExplore The InterpreterTuvaluAustralia and Tuvalu’s Falepili Union was only half the answer31 July 2026Sarah ThompsonGender & equalityAustralia’s Women, Peace and Security bill comes due30 July 2026Michelle Higelin South KoreaAustralia’s Pacific diplomacy has lessons – and limits – for South Korea30 July 2026Gabriela BernalMore on Pacific IslandsExplore Pacific IslandsEvent Replay2026 Allan Gyngell Lecture: Senator Penny WongPenny Wong, Michael Fullilove, Steven M.
